title: Maths for Machine Learning
tagline: Linear algebra, calculus, probability, information theory and optimisation for machine learning
summary: Machine learning is applied mathematics. This course collects the linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, information theory and optimisation that the rest of the atlas uses, always with an eye on how they appear inside neural networks and language models.
overview: Every operation inside a language model is a piece of mathematics: a token becomes a vector, a layer is a matrix multiplication followed by a nonlinearity, the output is a probability distribution over the vocabulary, and training minimises a cross-entropy loss by gradient descent. This course collects the mathematics the rest of the atlas relies on — linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, estimation, information theory and optimisation — and presents each topic through the role it plays in machine learning.

It starts with vectors, matrices and tensors as the data structures of deep learning, then the decompositions — eigenvalues, the singular value decomposition, low rank — that explain why weight matrices can be compressed. Calculus is reduced to what training needs: gradients, Jacobians and the chain rule that backpropagation automates. The probability chapters build distributions, expectation, Bayes’ rule and maximum likelihood; information theory defines entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence, the quantities a language model’s loss measures. The last chapter treats optimisation: convexity, gradient descent, stochastic gradients and momentum.

What makes this material hard is not any single result but keeping track of shapes, indices and probabilistic meaning at the same time. Work through small examples by hand and check every formula numerically — with NumPy or PyTorch this is a one-line habit — and use the figures to watch projections, gradients and distributions change as you move them.
outcomes: Manipulate vectors, matrices and tensors, and read a matrix product both as a composition of linear maps and as a batch of dot products.
Compute eigendecompositions and singular value decompositions, and use the SVD to find the best low-rank approximation of a matrix.
Derive gradients and Jacobians of vector-valued functions with the multivariable chain rule.
Work with common discrete and continuous distributions, expectations, conditional probability and Bayes’ rule.
Derive maximum-likelihood and maximum a posteriori estimators, and explain bias and variance.
Compute entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence, and explain why minimising cross-entropy fits a model to data.
Analyse gradient descent on convex and non-convex objectives, and explain the effect of the learning rate, stochastic gradients and momentum.

chapters.title: Vectors, matrices and tensors
chapters.summary: Vectors and matrices as data, matrix multiplication as composition, tensors and their shapes, and what linear algebra costs on hardware.

chapters.title: Eigenvalues, SVD and low rank
chapters.summary: Eigendecompositions, the singular value decomposition, low-rank approximation and why weight matrices can be compressed.

chapters.title: Gradients and the chain rule
chapters.summary: Partial derivatives, gradients and Jacobians, the multivariable chain rule and identities of matrix calculus.

chapters.title: Probability for machine learning
chapters.summary: Random variables, common distributions, expectation, conditional probability, Bayes’ rule and sampling.

chapters.title: Estimation and likelihood
chapters.summary: Maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori estimation, bias and variance, and the statistics of evaluation.

chapters.title: Information theory
chapters.summary: Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information, and why language models minimise cross-entropy.

chapters.title: Optimisation
chapters.summary: Convexity, gradient descent and its convergence, stochastic gradients, momentum and constrained optimisation.

history.title: The method of least squares
history.detail: Legendre published least squares for fitting comet orbits to observations; in 1809 Gauss justified it by assuming normally distributed errors.

history.title: Gradient descent
history.detail: Cauchy proposed solving systems of equations by repeatedly stepping against the gradient — the method of steepest descent that, in stochastic form, trains neural networks today.

history.title: The best low-rank approximation
history.detail: Eckart and Young proved that truncating the singular value decomposition gives the closest matrix of a given rank, the result behind low-rank compression and adapters such as LoRA.

history.title: A mathematical theory of communication
history.detail: Shannon defined entropy as the average information produced by a source, and generated text from the letter and word statistics of English — the first n-gram language models.

history.title: The Kullback–Leibler divergence
history.detail: Kullback and Leibler introduced a directed divergence between two distributions, now used to compare a model with data and to keep a fine-tuned model close to its starting point.

history.title: Stochastic approximation
history.detail: Robbins and Monro showed how to find the root of a function from noisy measurements with decreasing step sizes; applied to a gradient, this is stochastic gradient descent.

history.title: Momentum
history.detail: Polyak’s heavy-ball method added a fraction of the previous step to each update, accelerating gradient descent on ill-conditioned problems.
